del3-f4.title: Options
del3-f4.merke: Som H2025 E1: opsjonsintuisjon uten regning, med et handlingsråd
del3-f4.body:
Skarvheim Air ASA must hedge the jet fuel it will buy in one year. Fuel trades at $80 per barrel; treat it like a stock without dividends. The one-year risk-free rate is rf = 4%. The board requires one of two hedges:

  • (A) buy a one-year European call with strike K = $90, trading at $10.20;
  • (B) buy the same call and write (sell) a one-year European put with strike K = $70, trading at $6.36.

Applying Black-Scholes, you find that both prices imply σ = 40%. Just before you sign, your risk team tells you that the true annualised volatility is 30%, not 40%.

How would using the true volatility affect the fair prices of the call and the put? Considering the difference between the market prices and the fair prices, which hedge should Skarvheim choose and why? (You do not need any calculations to answer this question. Please answer both questions, each is worth 6 points; 4-6 sentences should typically be enough.)
del3-f4.solution:
Question 1: the true volatility lowers both fair prices. In the Black-Scholes setting the value of an option rises with volatility, for calls and puts alike. The reason is that the payoff is one-sided: the call pays max(ST − K, 0) and the put max(K − ST, 0), so a wider spread of the fuel price adds payoff in the tail where the option pays while the holder can never lose more than the premium in the other tail. The $10.20 and the $6.36 are by construction the Black-Scholes values at σ = 40%: that is what an implied volatility of 40% means. With σ = 30% both the call and the put are worth less than their market prices: both are overpriced.

Question 2: choose hedge B. With hedge A Skarvheim pays the whole overpricing of the call. With hedge B it pays the same overpricing on the call but recovers most of it, because it sells the put for more than the put is worth. Both hedges cap the fuel cost at $90; B also gives up the saving if fuel falls below $70, but at the true volatility that trade-off is priced fairly, so what separates the two hedges is the mispricing. Minimum accepted answer: do not buy the plain call (A) at $10.20. Full marks: choose B, since writing the overpriced put finances most of the overpriced call.

The numbers behind it (not required by the question). Black-Scholes with S = 80, rf = 4% (continuously compounded) and T = 1 year:

σCall, K = 90Put, K = 70Cost of ANet cost of B
40% (market)10.206.3610.203.84
30% (true)7.023.827.023.20

Per barrel hedge A pays about $3.19 more than it is worth, hedge B only about $0.64 (3.19 overpaid on the call less 2.54 overcharged on the put).

Caveats worth one sentence. This is not arbitrage: it is a bet that the risk team's estimate beats the market's. A hedge with a forward or futures contract, whose price does not depend on volatility, would avoid the mispricing altogether; it lies outside the two hedges the board approved, so it is a bonus remark, not the answer.

Also accepted. Naming vega for the sensitivity to volatility; the edge case σ = 0 to show why volatility has value for an option holder; the point that a trader without a hedging need would write both options and delta-hedge. Not enough on its own: «B is better because it is cheaper ($3.84 against $10.20)». A lower premium says nothing about value, because B also gives up the saving below $70.
criteria: Question 1 (6 points): 2 for stating that the fair call price is LOWER at 30%, 2 for stating that the fair put price is also LOWER, 2 for the reason: the payoff is one-sided, so more dispersion adds upside without adding downside to the holder. A direction without a reason earns no reason points.

Counting in question 1: the call and the put share one mechanism, so one well-explained reason covers both. «Vega» and «convexity» are one reason, not two. Saying the put gains when volatility falls is the classic error.

Question 2 (6 points): 2 for recognising that the market prices are the Black-Scholes values at the implied 40%, so both options are overpriced relative to the true fair value; 2 for rejecting the plain call A (the minimum accepted answer, as in the H2025 key: «at a minimum not buy»); 2 for choosing B because the written put is sold for more than it is worth and so recovers most of the overpricing.
«B is cheaper» without the mispricing argument earns at most 2 of the 6 points in question 2: the lower net premium is paid for by giving up the saving below $70.
Answers both questions explicitly. An answer that discusses only the volatility effect and never chooses a hedge loses the second 6 points.
No calculation is required; a purely verbal answer scores full marks. Numbers, the not-arbitrage caveat and the forward-contract remark are a bonus.

del3-f4.title: Governance
del3-f4.merke: Som H2024 E2: to måter å overvåke ledelsen på
del3-f4.body:
Tallowfield Retail Inc. is a US-listed chain of home-improvement stores with dispersed ownership: no shareholder owns more than 2% of the shares. The CEO has run the company for eleven years and also chairs the board. Same-store sales have fallen for three years, yet the board has approved all six acquisitions the CEO has proposed and was re-elected last year without a single competing candidate. The corporate travel budget has doubled.

Select and describe two distinct ways of monitoring the CEO: one performed inside the firm (by people who sit on its board or work for it) and one performed from outside the firm. For each, explain who is performing the monitoring and which tools they have at their disposal. Take Tallowfield's situation into account. (Limit your explanations to 3-4 sentences per method at most; each method is worth 6 points.)
del3-f4.solution:
Two methods, 6 points each: about 2 for who monitors and why that monitor has the power or the incentive. The other 4 are for the tools, applied to Tallowfield.

Inside: the board of directors, acting through its independent directors. The board is elected by the shareholders and takes the key decisions: it hires and fires the CEO, sets the pay through the compensation committee, approves the budget, large spending and acquisitions. It also has the best access to internal reports and files. At Tallowfield the CEO chairs the board, which is the red flag: the CEO sets the agenda of the body that is supposed to monitor the CEO. The independent directors can still act by meeting in executive session without the CEO, appointing a lead independent director, demanding the travel figures and a post-deal review of the six acquisitions through the audit committee and, as a majority, separating the chair from the CEO or replacing the CEO.

Outside: institutional investors and activist shareholders. With no holder above 2%, a small investor gains too little to pay for monitoring and free-rides, so the monitor is a large institution (a pension fund, a mutual fund) or an activist hedge fund that builds a stake big enough to make the effort pay. Its tools are requesting information and meeting management, voting against the directors and against the pay package (say on pay) and submitting shareholder proposals, for example for an independent chair. If management ignores it, the investor can start a public activist campaign and a proxy fight: after an election without competing candidates, its own slate would give the shareholders a real choice.

Other methods that score equally. Inside: employees and internal audit, who can report misuse to the audit committee, go around a corrupt boss or, as a last resort, go to the media. Outside: the market for corporate control, where three years of falling sales make Tallowfield a takeover target and a bidder can buy the firm and install a more efficient management (even the threat disciplines the CEO); lenders, through covenants and demands for information; the government, through disclosure rules, regulators, anti-fraud agencies and the courts; external auditors; analysts and the financial press.

What the H2024 key accepts. Its channels are the board, the shareholders themselves, the government and external monitoring through the market. It gives full points for any two groups described in enough detail.
criteria: Two methods, 6 points each: about 2 for WHO monitors (and why that monitor has the power or the incentive) and 4 for WHICH TOOLS they have. An answer that describes a mechanism without naming the monitor, or names the monitor without its tools, loses those points.

One method inside the firm and one outside, as asked. Two genuinely distinct methods from the same side (inside or outside): full points for one, at most 3 for the other. Two versions of the same tool, such as «the board» and «the compensation committee», are one method: the second earns 0.

Accepted inside: the board and its independent directors and committees; employees and internal audit. Accepted outside: institutional investors, blockholders and activists; the market for corporate control; lenders through covenants; government and regulators; external auditors; analysts and the press.

Use the situation: about 1 of the 4 tool points of each method. Board: say how it can monitor although the CEO chairs it (independent directors, executive sessions without the CEO, a lead independent director, separating the roles). Kurbatov calls the CEO as chair «the only red flag» while a CEO seat on the board is fine (lecture 13, recording 17, 40:44). Shareholders: no holder above 2% means small holders free-ride, so the monitor is an institution or an activist with a larger stake.
Tools must be explained, not listed: five tool names without what they do earn at most half of the tool points.
3-4 sentences per method at most, as instructed. Length is not rewarded.

del3-f5.title: M&A
del3-f5.merke: Som H2024 E1: fire grunner, positivt og negativt for kjøper og mål
del3-f5.body:
Østfold Bakeri ASA, a large listed Norwegian bakery group, makes a friendly all-cash offer for Lundqvist Bröd AB, a listed Swedish bakery chain, at a premium of 35% over Lundqvist's share price. Lundqvist's founder has run the company for 30 years and will retire once the deal is completed.

Give four possible reasons, one for each case: why this deal could be positive for Østfold, negative for Østfold, positive for Lundqvist and negative for Lundqvist (for Lundqvist, consider its shareholders, its employees or the firm itself). Reasons must be other than «synergies». «Value creation» without a mechanism does not count as a reason. Keep explanations short, 1-2 sentences per reason (3 points per reason).
del3-f5.solution:
Four boxes, one reason each, one to two sentences each, three points per box. Synergies are banned, so each reason below rests on information, access, agency or a transfer of value.

1. Positive for Østfold: a foothold in a new market. Building a Swedish chain from scratch means licences, shop sites, suppliers and staff; buying Lundqvist gives Østfold an established brand, its customers and its relations with Swedish authorities at once.

2. Negative for Østfold: empire building. Managers whose pay and prestige grow with the size of the group may buy for size rather than for value. If the 35% cash premium is not earned back, value moves from Østfold's shareholders to Lundqvist's, which is why acquirers see negative announcement returns in about half of all deals.

3. Positive for Lundqvist: the control premium. Lundqvist's shareholders receive 35% above the market price, in cash and at once; since a target can always say no, it has the bargaining power and captures most of the gains from a deal.

4. Negative for Lundqvist: loss of the founder's vision and damage to the corporate culture. The firm loses the person whose long-term plan built it. Integration into a large group's procedures can destroy the culture that made the chain work, while the new owner may bend long-term plans towards quick returns to justify the premium.

Other defensible answers. Positive for Østfold: market power (a larger share of the Nordic market, fewer competitors), supply-chain control, access to scarce resources such as Lundqvist's shop sites or recipes, buying a target the market undervalues when Østfold has better information, a disciplinary gain from replacing weaker management. Negative for Østfold: hubris and the winner's curse (the most optimistic bidder wins and overpays), integration costs and a clash of cultures, the market reading a cash bid as a sign that the managers see no better use for the cash. Positive for Lundqvist: better management and more efficient practices, access to the parent's capital and to larger or different markets, a solved succession problem now that the founder retires, economies of scale when explained by a mechanism such as fixed costs spread over more volume or stronger purchasing power (the H2024 key lists economies of scale for the target; cost cuts from merging two departments alone are synergies, recording 16, 3:50 and 11:09). Negative for Lundqvist: layoffs and loss of key staff, loss of independence, a cash payment that triggers capital-gains tax for the shareholders at once, a founder who wants out and accepts too low a bid.

Not accepted. Buying Lundqvist for its tax losses: Kurbatov notes that the losses are erased when the firm changes owner (recording 17, 1:14:01). «Value creation» or «the firms are worth more together» without a mechanism: Kurbatov says this «wouldn't be really accepted during the exam» (recording 16, 11:39).
criteria: Exactly four reasons, one in each box: positive for Østfold, negative for Østfold, positive for Lundqvist, negative for Lundqvist. Graded box by box, 3 points each, so an empty box loses a quarter of the points.

Synergies are banned and «value creation» without a mechanism earns nothing. Any other reasonable reason with a sufficient explanation is accepted (H2024 key: the list is not exhaustive), including market power and supply-chain considerations. Economies of scale count only with a mechanism (fixed costs spread over more volume, purchasing power); cost cuts from merging departments alone are synergies (recording 16, 3:50 and 11:09).
Each reason must be explained in 1-2 sentences: a name alone («hubris», «culture») earns at most 1 of 3 points.

Two close reasons: the premium as a gain for Lundqvist's shareholders and «Østfold overpays» as a loss for Østfold. Overpayment explained as a wealth transfer from Østfold's to Lundqvist's shareholders earns 2 of 3; overpayment with a cause of its own (empire building, hubris, the winner's curse) earns 3 of 3. «Østfold pays too much» with no explanation earns 1 of 3.

Use the deal: the Swedish market (foothold), the cash premium (capital-gains tax at once) and the retiring founder (loss of vision and culture, a solved succession, a founder who accepts too low a bid) are the natural hooks. Generic reasons earn full points if explained, but naming the mechanism is what sensor rewards.
Tax losses are not an accepted motive: they are erased on a change of owner (Kurbatov, recording 17).

del3-f5.title: Governance
del3-f5.merke: Som H2025 E2: tre tiltak for en eier med 5–10 %
del3-f5.body:
You manage a pension fund that owns 7% of the shares of Quillfield Outfitters Inc., a US-listed chain of outdoor-clothing stores whose other shares are widely dispersed. For five years Quillfield has held about $2 billion in cash that earns less than 1% a year. The CEO refuses to pay out the cash or to say what it is for, while the company has bought a corporate jet and sponsors a golf tournament where the CEO hosts friends. Analysts see no profitable expansion projects in Quillfield's markets.

What are possible actions you could undertake? Select 3 such actions and briefly explain (2-3 sentences per action, each action is worth 4 points).
del3-f5.solution:
The setting is the manager-shareholder agency problem in its free-cash-flow form: idle cash with no good projects funds the CEO's private benefits. The 7% stake matters: the fund keeps 7 cents of every dollar of value it restores, enough to pay for monitoring that a 0.01% holder would leave to others, but not enough to give orders. Three actions in the 2-3 sentence format:

1. Engage the board and propose a payout. I demand meetings with the independent directors and file a shareholder proposal for a special dividend or a share repurchase. A firm should invest its cash only if there are good investment opportunities; here analysts see none, so paying it out removes the money that funds the jet and the tournament.

2. Push for a new compensation contract for the CEO. Through the compensation committee and a vote against the pay package (say on pay), I press for pay in restricted shares with long vesting, so that the CEO's wealth rises only with long-run share value. Perks such as the jet are then paid partly out of the CEO's own stake, so private benefits become costly to the CEO and not only to the shareholders.

3. Escalate: vote against the board, nominate directors and run a proxy fight. If quiet engagement fails, I vote my 7% against the directors who approved the spending, publish a letter with a plan for the cash, solicit proxies from the other institutions and run my own slate of directors at the annual meeting (through proxy access if Quillfield's bylaws allow it). With 7% plus the support of other institutions a proxy fight is winnable; the threat alone often makes the board act.

Other actions that score. Making the board more independent by replacing insider directors; pressing to fire the CEO; a debt-financed recapitalisation, so that interest payments commit the cash; supporting or finding an acquirer, or an LBO that replaces the management; legal action if there is good evidence that company money is spent for private purposes; and, as a bonus for creativity in the H2025 key, exiting by selling the shares.

Naming the channel. Each action belongs to one side of the governance system: internal monitoring (the board and its committees), the shareholder's own toolkit (voice, votes, proposals, proxy fights, litigation, exit) or the market for corporate control.
criteria: Exactly three actions, 2-3 sentences each, 4 points each, graded independently.

As in the H2025 key, any reasonable action with an explanation is accepted: active monitoring and engagement, an activist campaign, a more independent board, a better compensation contract, voting or pressing to fire the CEO, an LBO or a friendly acquirer, legal action with good evidence and, as a bonus for creativity, exit by selling.

Use the situation: idle cash and no profitable projects. A payout action earns full points with the condition, the same logic as recording 05 (14:34): invest the cash only if there are good investment opportunities; otherwise pay it out. «Pay a dividend» without that condition earns at most 3 of 4.
Use the 7% stake: large enough to overcome the free-rider problem in monitoring, too small for control. An answer that would read identically for a 0.01% holder is weaker.

Counting: «vote against the directors» and «run a proxy fight to replace them» count as one action unless each gets its own mechanism (the first is a signal at the annual meeting, the second a contest with its own slate and solicitation). A dividend and a repurchase are one action (a payout).
Naming the channel (internal monitoring, shareholder voice, market for corporate control) is rewarded.

del3-f6.title: Options
del3-f6.merke: Som H2025 E1, ny vinkel: opsjonsintuisjon uten regning
del3-f6.body:
You hold a large position in Bjørnnes Gruve ASA, a listed mining company whose share trades at NOK 150 and pays no dividends. A court will rule on Bjørnnes's main mining licence within the next year. To protect the position you consider buying one-year European put options with strike K = NOK 140, which trade at NOK 7.72. The one-year risk-free rate is 4%. Applying Black-Scholes, you find that the market price implies σ = 25%. Your own analysis of the court case suggests that the true annualised volatility over the year is closer to 40%.

a) How would the true volatility affect the fair price of the put? (4 points)

b) Considering the difference between the market price and your fair price, what should you do? (4 points)

c) Your broker also offers an American put with the same strike and expiry. Is its fair value higher, lower or the same as that of the European put? Does your volatility argument in b) also apply to the American put? (4 points)

(You do not need any calculations to answer these questions. 2-3 sentences per question should be enough.)
del3-f6.solution:
a) The fair price of the put is higher than NOK 7.72. In the Black-Scholes setting an option's value rises with volatility, for puts as for calls, because the payoff max(K − ST, 0) is one-sided: a wider spread makes a deep fall below NOK 140 (the licence is lost) more likely, while the holder never loses more than the premium if the share rises. Since σ enters nowhere else, replacing 25% by 40% can only raise the value.

b) Buy the put. The NOK 7.72 is by construction the Black-Scholes value at the implied 25%, so if your estimate is right the put is underpriced: you buy the protection for less than it is worth, roughly half of its fair value. The minimum correct answer is to buy the put; a stronger answer adds that you should not pay for it by writing calls on your shares, since a call priced at 25% would be underpriced too and you would be selling cheaply what you believe is valuable.

c) The American put is worth at least as much, in practice more; the volatility argument applies to it too. It gives every right of the European put plus the right to exercise early. For a put that right has value even without dividends: if the share collapses after a ruling, exercising at once gives you NOK 140 today instead of in a year. Higher volatility raises the American put's value too, so if its market price also reflects 25% it is also underpriced by your estimate. A higher price for the American put is not by itself a sign that it is expensive: compare each price with its own fair value.

The numbers behind it (not required). Black-Scholes with S = 150, K = 140, rf = 4% (continuously compounded) and T = 1: the put is worth NOK 7.72 at σ = 25% and NOK 15.63 at σ = 40%.

Also accepted. The edge case σ = 0, where an out-of-the-money put would be worthless; naming vega; the caveat that this is not arbitrage but a bet that your estimate beats the market's; noting that the court ruling is a jump, which the lognormal assumption behind Black-Scholes does not capture, so one σ describes the risk only roughly; Kurbatov's rule of thumb that an option which gives more rights is priced higher (recording 12, 12:41). Only the direction is asked in c): no pricing of the American put is expected (recording 18, 58:09).
criteria: a) 4 points: 2 for the direction (the fair price is HIGHER than the market price, because option values rise with volatility for puts as well as calls), 2 for the one-sided payoff reason. Saying the put loses value because «higher volatility helps the call» is the classic error.

b) 4 points: 2 for recognising that the market price is the Black-Scholes value at the implied 25%, so the put is underpriced by your estimate; 2 for the action. Minimum accepted answer: buy the put. Not financing it by writing calls is a bonus.

c) 4 points: 2 for «at least as much» or «higher» with the reason (it contains the European put plus the right to exercise early; receiving K earlier has value); «the same» earns no direction points, since that holds for calls without dividends, not for puts. 2 for «yes»: higher volatility raises the American put's value too, so the argument in b) carries over.
Counting in c): «more flexibility» and «early exercise» are one reason, not two.
Answers every question explicitly. An answer that discusses volatility only and never states an action loses the points in b).
No calculation is required and none is expected; a purely verbal answer scores full marks. Bonus: the court ruling is a jump that the lognormal model behind Black-Scholes does not capture.

del3-f6.title: Governance
del3-f6.merke: Som H2025 E2 i formen: tre tiltak, nå fra eierens side
del3-f6.body:
The Hollowmere family owns 60% of Hollowmere Therapeutics Inc., a US-listed company that develops cancer drugs. Each drug takes about ten years and many risky trials before it earns anything. For the first time the family will hire a CEO from outside the family. It wants the new CEO to act in the shareholders' interest, but it does not want to monitor so harshly that the CEO avoids every risk.

You advise the family. Select three measures it could put in place and briefly explain, for each, how it makes the CEO act in the shareholders' interest and why it does not scare the CEO away from valuable risks. (2-3 sentences per measure, each measure is worth 4 points.)
del3-f6.solution:
Three measures, each answering both halves of the question: alignment and room for valuable risk. The firm's ten-year, high-risk projects are the key fact: a design that rewards this year's numbers would make the CEO cut trials.

1. Pay in shares and options that vest over many years, not an EPS bonus. Restricted shares and options with five- to seven-year vesting tie the CEO's wealth to the long-run value of the drug pipeline. An option pays only on the upside, so it rewards taking good risks, while an annual EPS target would invite cutting trials or buying back shares to lift EPS, the short-termism Kurbatov warns about (recording 17, 37:19).

2. A golden parachute or an employment guarantee. A severance package if the CEO is dismissed without misconduct means that a failed trial does not end the CEO's career at a loss, so the CEO is not afraid to start long, risky projects. It should be capped and tied to the absence of misconduct, so that it does not simply reward failure.

3. An independent board of about 7 to 11 directors with the CEO as a member but not as chair. The family nominates some directors and recruits independent ones with industry knowledge; the board hires and fires the CEO and approves funding trial by trial, at the milestones, rather than second-guessing daily decisions. A CEO seat on the board keeps the CEO informed and involved; the red flag would be the CEO also chairing it.

Other measures that score. Transparency and better communication: regular reports on each trial, press releases and meetings with the other shareholders. Funding projects in stages, so that each new stage needs the board's approval. ESG metrics, which Kurbatov calls «much less abusable» than EPS (recording 17, 38:23). Milestone targets tied to trial progress are also accepted (recording 17, 37:10), with clauses that stop short-term abuse (37:19). The family voting its 60% at the annual meeting and keeping control through dual-class shares, with both sides argued: control and a long horizon against entrenchment and weaker outside monitoring.

Why not maximal monitoring. Monitor too harshly and the CEO does only the bare minimum; do not monitor at all and the CEO may abuse the position. The three measures aim between the two, as the question asks.
criteria: Three measures, 2-3 sentences each, 4 points each: 2 for how it aligns the CEO with the shareholders and 2 for why it keeps valuable risk-taking. The question asks for both; an answer that gives only the alignment earns at most 2 of 4 per measure.

Accepted measures (lecture 13): long-horizon equity pay; options; a golden parachute or employment guarantee; an independent board; the CEO on the board but not as chair; transparency and communication; staged funding with milestone reviews; ESG metrics («much less abusable» than EPS, recording 17, 38:23); milestone targets tied to trial progress (37:10) with clauses that stop short-term abuse (37:19); the family's own voting and nomination power; dual-class shares with both sides.
Use the situation: ten-year, risky R&D. An annual EPS or profit bonus without a guard against short-termism earns at most 1 of 4, since it pushes the CEO to cut trials or buy back shares.
Counting: options and restricted shares are one measure (equity pay); an independent board and a separate chair are one measure unless each gets its own mechanism.
Board size: Kurbatov's range is 7 to 11 (recording 17, 34:46). «A smaller board works better» is not an accepted reason; too small lacks capacity and too large invites free-riding.
Golden parachute: accepted with the risk-taking argument (recording 17, 16:18). Calling it only entrenchment misses the question; noting that it can reward failure is a bonus.
